questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-11{x}^{2}+9x+18.$ We know that $(x-2)$ and $(x-3)$ are factors of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-3)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-3)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-11$ | $9$ | $18$ |
|  | $↓$ | $3$ | $6$ | $-15$ | $-18$ |
|  | $1$ | $2$ | $-5$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-11{x}^{2}+9x+18}{x-3}={x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-5x-6,
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-11{x}^{2}+9x+18=(x-3)({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-5x-6).
$$

Now, because $(x-2)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-5x-6).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x-2)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-5$ | $-6$ |
|  | $↓$ | $2$ | $8$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $4$ | $3$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-5x-6}{x-2}={x}^{2}+4x+3,
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-11{x}^{2}+9x+18=(x-2)(x-3)({x}^{2}+4x+3).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-11{x}^{2}+9x+18=(x-2)(x-3){{(x+1)(x+3)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=(x+1)(x+3).$

questions.problem: Let $p(x)={x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-35{x}^{2}-57x+90.$ Given that $p(-3)=p(1)=0,$ find the sum of all distinct real roots of $p(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $p(-3)=p(1)=0,$ by factor theorem $(x+3)$ and $(x-1)$ are both factors of $p(x).$
To factor $p(x)$ completely we need to find its other factors.

Since $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-35$ | $-57$ | $90$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-33$ | $-90$ |
|  | $1$ | $2$ | $-33$ | $-90$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-35{x}^{2}-57x+90}{x-1}={x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-33x-90,
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-35{x}^{2}-57x+90=(x-1)({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-33x-90).
$$

Now, because $(x+3)$ is also a factor of $p(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-33x-90).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x+3)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-3$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-33$ | $-90$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-3$ | $3$ | $90$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-30$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-33x-90}{x+3}={x}^{2}-x-30,
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-35{x}^{2}-57x+90=(x-1)(x+3)({x}^{2}-x-30).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-35{x}^{2}-57x+90=(x-1)(x+3)(x-6)(x+5).
$$

We can now equate each factor to zero and solve for $x$ to find the three roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1\,,\,x=-3\,,\,x=6\,,\,x=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the sum of the roots of the polynomial is

$$
1-3+6-5=-1.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x-2.$ We know that $(x-2)$ and $(x+1)$ are factors of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-2)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-2)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $-2$ |
|  | $↓$ | $4$ | $2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
|  | $2$ | $1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x-2}{x-2}=2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+1,
$$

which means that

$$
2{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x-2=(x-2)(2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+1).
$$

Now, because $(x+1)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $(2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+1).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $0$ | $1$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $-1$ |
|  | $2$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+1}{x+1}=2{x}^{2}-x+1,
$$

which means that

$$
2{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x-2=(x-2)(x+1)(2{x}^{2}-x+1).
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-x+1$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac=(-1)^{2}-4(2)(1)=-7<0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-x+1$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative. 

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by 

$$
2{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x-2=(x-2)(x+1){{(2{x}^{2}-x+1)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Finally, $P(x)=2{x}^{2}-x+1.$

Let $f(x)=-3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+30{x}^{2}-7x+60.$ We know that $(x+3)$ and $(x-4)$ are factors of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.  

Because $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x+3)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+3)$ using synthetic division:  

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-3$ | $-3$ | $4$ | $30$ | $-7$ | $60$ |
|  | $↓$ | $9$ | $-39$ | $27$ | $-60$ |
|  | $-3$ | $13$ | $-9$ | $20$ | $0$ |

Therefore,  

$$
\frac{-3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+30{x}^{2}-7x+60}{x+3}=-3{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-9x+20,
$$

which means that  

$$
-3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+30{x}^{2}-7x+60=(x+3)(-3{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-9x+20).
$$

Now, because $(x-4)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $(-3{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-9x+20).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division once more:  

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $-3$ | $13$ | $-9$ | $20$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-12$ | $4$ | $-20$ |
|  | $-3$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $0$ |

Therefore,  

$$
\frac{-3{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-9x+20}{x-4}=-3{x}^{2}+x-5,
$$

which means that  

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+30{x}^{2}-7x+60 & =(x+3)(x-4)(-3{x}^{2}+x-5) \\  & =-(x+3)(x-4)(3{x}^{2}-x+5).\end{aligned}
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial $3{x}^{2}-x+5$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:  

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac=(-1)^{2}-4(3)(5)=-59<0.
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial $3{x}^{2}-x+5$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative.  

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by  

$$
-3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+30{x}^{2}-7x+60=-(x+3)(x-4){{(3{x}^{2}-x+5)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Finally, $P(x)=3{x}^{2}-x+5.$

$$

Finally, $P(x)={x}^{2}+1.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}+34{x}^{2}-90x+225.$ We know that $(x-5)^{2}$ is a factor of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-5)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $5$ | $1$ | $-10$ | $34$ | $-90$ | $225$ |
|  | $↓$ | $5$ | $-25$ | $45$ | $-225$ |
|  | $1$ | $-5$ | $9$ | $-45$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}+34{x}^{2}-90x+225}{x-5}={x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}+9x-45,
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}+34{x}^{2}-90x+225=(x-5)({x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}+9x-45).
$$

Now, because $(x-5)^{2}$ is a factor of $f(x),$ $(x-5)$ must be also a factor of the quotient $({x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}+9x-45).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $5$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $9$ | $-45$ |
|  | $↓$ | $5$ | $0$ | $45$ |
|  | $1$ | $0$ | $9$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}+9x-45}{x-2}={x}^{2}+9,
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}+34{x}^{2}-90x+225=(x-5)^{2}({x}^{2}+9).
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2}+9$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac={0}^{2}-4(1)(9)=-36<0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2}+9$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative. 

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by 

$$
{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}+34{x}^{2}-90x+225=(x-5)^{2}{{({x}^{2}+9)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Finally, $P(x)={x}^{2}+9.$

Let $f(x)=2{x}^{4}-7{x}^{3}-34{x}^{2}+56x-192.$ We know that $(x+4)$ and $(x-6)$ are factors of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x+4)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+4)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-4$ | $2$ | $-7$ | $-34$ | $56$ | $-192$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-8$ | $60$ | $-104$ | $192$ |
|  | $2$ | $-15$ | $26$ | $-48$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{4}-7{x}^{3}-34{x}^{2}+56x-192}{x+4}=2{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+26x-48,
$$

which means that

$$
2{x}^{4}-7{x}^{3}-34{x}^{2}+56x-192=(x+4)(2{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+26x-48).
$$

Now, because $(x-6)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $(2{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+26x-48).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x-6)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $6$ | $2$ | $-15$ | $26$ | $-48$ |
|  | $↓$ | $12$ | $-18$ | $48$ |
|  | $2$ | $-3$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+26x-48}{x-6}=2{x}^{2}-3x+8,
$$

which means that

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{4}-7{x}^{3}-34{x}^{2}+56x-192 & =(x+4)(x-6)(2{x}^{2}-3x+8)\end{aligned}
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-3x+8$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac=(-3)^{2}-4(2)(8)=-55<0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-3x+8$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative. 

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by 

$$
2{x}^{4}-7{x}^{3}-34{x}^{2}+56x-192=(x+4)(x-6){{(2{x}^{2}-3x+8)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Finally, $P(x)=2{x}^{2}-3x+8.$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $(x-1)$ and $(x-3)$ are factors of the polynomial $f(x)= x^4 - x^3 - 7 x^2 + x + 6,$ factor $f(x)$ completely.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To factor $f(x)$ completely, we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | $x^4$ | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-7$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
|  | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{x^4 - x^3 - 7 x^2 + x + 6}{x-1} = x^3-7x-6,
$$

which means that

$$
x^4 - x^3 - 7 x^2 + x + 6 = (x-1) (x^3-7x-6).
$$

Now, because $(x-3)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $(x^3-7x-6).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x-3)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}3$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $3$ | $9$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{x^3-7x-6}{x-3} = x^2+3x +2,
$$

which means that

$$
x^4 - x^3 - 7 x^2 + x + 6 =  (x-1) (x-3) (x^2+3x +2).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
x^4 - x^3 - 7 x^2 + x + 6 =  (x-1) (x-3) (x+2)(x+1).
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $p(x) = x^4 - x^3 - 9 x^2 - 11 x - 4.$ Knowing that $p(4) = p(-1) = 0,$ factor the polynomial $p(x)$ completely.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $p(4) = p(-1) = 0,$ the factor theorem guarantees that $(x - 4)$ and $(x + 1)$ are both factors of $p(x).$
To factor $p(x)$ completely, we need to find its other factors.

Since $(x - 4)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x - 4)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x - 4)$ using synthetic division:

|  | $x^4$ | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}4$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-9$ | $-11$ | $-4$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $4$ | $12$ | $12$ | $4$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $3$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{x^4 - x^3 - 9 x^2 - 11 x - 4}{x-4} = x^3+3x^2+3x+1,
$$

which means that

$$
x^4 - x^3 - 9 x^2 - 11 x - 4 = (x-4) (  x^3+3x^2+3x+1).
$$

Now, because $(x+1)$ is also a factor of $p(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $( x^3+3x^2+3x+1).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}-1$ | $1$ | $3$ | $3$ | $1$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $-1$ | $-2$ | $-1$ |
|  | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{ x^3+3x^2+3x-1}{x+1} = x^2+2x+1,
$$

which means that

$$
x^4 - x^3 - 9 x^2 - 11 x - 4 = (x-4)(x+1)(x^2+2x+1).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}-11x-4 & =(x-4)(x+1)(x+1)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)(x+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x) = 3 x^4 - 5 x^3 - 3 x^2 + 6 x - 8.$ If $x=2$ and $x=-\dfrac{4}{3}$ are zeros of $f(x),$ factor $f(x)$ completely.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Because $x=2$ and $x=-\dfrac{4}{3}$ are both zeros of $f(x),$ the factor theorem guarantees that $(x-2)$ and $\left( x + \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ are both factors of $f(x).$ So, $(x-2)$ and $\left( x + \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ both divide $f(x).$

To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by one of these factors (it doesn't matter which one we divide first). Let's divide $f(x)$ by $(x-2)$ using synthetic division:

|  | $x^4$ | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}2$ | $3$ | $-5$ | $-3$ | $6$ | $-8$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $6$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $8$ |
|  | $3$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $4$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3{x}^{4}-5{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\  & =(x-2)(3{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, because $\left( x+\dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $3x^3 + x^2 - x +4.$ So, we divide this quotient by $\left( x+\dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}-\dfrac{4}{3}$ | $3$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $4$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $-4$ | $4$ | $-4$ |
|  | $3$ | $-3$ | $3$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x+4 & =(x+\frac{4}{3})(3{x}^{2}-3x+3) \\  & =(x+\frac{4}{3})(3)({x}^{2}-x+1) \\  & =(3x+4)({x}^{2}-x+1),\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{4}-5{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+6x-8 & =(x-2)(3x+4)({x}^{2}-x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

The quadratic polynomial $x^2-x+1$ does not appear to factor over the real numbers. We can make sure of this by verifying that its discriminant is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D={b}^{2}-4ac=(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1)=-3<0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by 

$$
f(x) = (x-2)(3x+4)(x^2-x+1).
$$
